content: Lectins are proteins that specifically bind to sugar molecules, demonstrating a high degree of specificity for their sugar moieties. These proteins are involved in various biological recognition processes, particularly those involving interactions between cells and proteins. For instance, certain bacteria utilize lectins to adhere to the cells of a host organism during the process of infection. The term lectin originates from the Latin word legere, which translates to to select. Although lectins were initially discovered over a century ago in plants, they are now recognized as being widespread throughout nature. The earliest documented description of a lectin-like hemagglutinin is attributed to Peter Hermann Stillmark, who described it in his 1888 doctoral thesis at the University of Dorpat (a prominent institution in czarist Russia). Stillmark isolated this hemagglutinin, which was also highly toxic, from the seeds of the castor tree (Ricinus communis), naming it ricin. Most lectins are non-enzymatic in their activity and are not derived from the immune system. They are found ubiquitously in nature and can bind either to soluble carbohydrates or to carbohydrate components of glycoproteins or glycolipids. Lectins are known to agglutinate certain animal cells and precipitate glycoconjugates. In animals, lectins perform a variety of functions. For example, lectins on the surface of mammalian liver cells specifically recognize galactose residues. These cell-surface receptors are believed to facilitate the removal of certain glycoproteins from the bloodstream. Another example is the mannose-6-phosphate receptor, which identifies hydrolytic enzymes containing mannose-6-phosphate residues and directs these enzymes to lysosomes. A defect in this system is associated with I-cell disease. Lectins also play roles in regulating cell adhesion, glycoprotein synthesis, and controlling protein levels in the blood. Additionally, lectins are integral to the immune system, where they recognize carbohydrates unique to pathogens or inaccessible on host cells. Examples include the lectin complement activation pathway and mannose-binding lectin. In plants, the precise function of lectins remains uncertain. While it was once hypothesized that lectins were essential for rhizobia binding, this theory was disproven through lectin-knockout transgene studies. The high concentration of lectins in plant seeds, which diminishes as the plant grows, suggests a role in seed germination and possibly in the survival of the seed itself. In the field of medicine, purified lectins are clinically significant, particularly in blood typing. Lectins can identify specific glycolipids and glycoproteins on the surface of red blood cells: A lectin from Dolichos biflorus is used to identify cells of the A1 blood group. A lectin from Ulex europaeus is used to detect the H blood group antigen. A lectin from Vicia graminea is used to identify the N blood group antigen. In neuroscience, the lectin PHA-L, derived from kidney beans, is employed to trace the pathways of efferent axons using a technique known as the anterograde labeling method. Lectins, particularly those from legume plants such as PHA or concanavalin A, have been extensively used as model systems to study how proteins recognize carbohydrates. These lectins are relatively easy to obtain and exhibit a wide range of sugar specificities. The numerous crystal structures of legume lectins have provided detailed insights into the atomic-level interactions between carbohydrates and proteins. One of the most striking examples of the biological potency of lectins is the biochemical warfare agent ricin. Ricin, derived from the seeds of the castor oil plant, consists of two functional domains: 1. A lectin domain that binds to galactosyl residues on cell surfaces, facilitating the protein's entry into cells. 2. An N-glycosidase domain that removes nucleobases from ribosomal RNA, thereby inhibiting protein synthesis and ultimately causing cell death.
